source.title: SAEmnesia: Erasing Concepts in Diffusion Models with Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: E. Cassano; Riccardo Renzulli; Marco Nurisso; Mirko Zaffaroni; A. Perotti; Marco Grangetto

record.tranche_reason: The study compares unsupervised and supervised SAE representations and measures whether concept information becomes concentrated in individual latents. This bears on training-dependent feature specialization, but it does not use the original studies’ neuron-interpretability methods.
record.gate_note: The study measures feature centralization and overlap between concept-assigned latents in diffusion-model SAEs. Unlearning accuracy, image quality, attack robustness, and timing results are not rows because they do not measure neuron polysemanticity or concept-feature concentration. The paper's discussion of polysemanticity in other work is not recorded as a result.
record.test_reason: The study builds a supervised SAE for concept erasure in Stable Diffusion and reports its own method against SAeUron. It does not measure how often the diffusion model's own neurons respond to unrelated inputs. All feature-score, k-NN and Cats-Dogs overlap results describe SAE latents shaped on purpose by supervised concept-assignment losses. They also mainly address feature splitting (one concept spread over many latents), which is the converse of polysemanticity. No version's construct is measured: neither V5's share of polysemantic network neurons under architecture or regularization changes, nor any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that supervised SAE training prevents feature splitting and gives one-to-one concept-latent mappings in SD v1.5. This yields better, cheaper concept erasure than unsupervised SAEs: 91.51% versus 82.29% on UnlearnCanvas objects, 96.67% less hyperparameter search, and better sequential unlearning. They acknowledge that semantically similar concepts within a group still interfere. Their framing concerns feature splitting in SAE latents, not polysemantic network neurons.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains supervised TopK SAEs on diffusion-model cross-attention activations and measures concept-score concentration and concept overlap; it does not reproduce the methods in the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature overlap varies substantially across SAE loss variants and between from-scratch and fine-tuned training; the paper reports some variants with zero Cats-Dogs overlap and others with baseline-level or higher overlap.

fits_no_version.finding: Supervised concept-assignment losses concentrate concept scores onto a single SAE latent. For Flowers, the max score is 0.0404 versus 0.0166 for an unsupervised SAE.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Supervised SAE training reduces feature splitting of concepts across SAE latents in diffusion models.

fits_no_version.finding: How often Cats and Dogs share a most-active SAE latent across timesteps varies by SAE loss variant. Overlap is 0 to 14 timesteps versus 10 for the unsupervised SAE.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Concept overlap in SAE latents of diffusion models depends on the SAE training objective and on fine-tuning versus training from scratch.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The measurements concern SAE latent features in diffusion-model activations, not individual neurons in the original pretrained network. The Cats-Dogs overlap test concerns two related object concepts and varies by training variant. The k-NN figure is not accompanied by exact values in the text. The reported standard deviations across four seeds concern benchmark unlearning metrics, not the feature-score or overlap measurements.
record.rows_left_out: Excluded the remaining concept-score histograms in Appendix A.6 because they are figure-only distributions without stated numerical outcomes, and excluded unlearning performance, FID, robustness, and runtime results because they do not measure neuron-feature concentration or polysemanticity.

untested.parts: No test of superposition as a cause.
No test of initialization, regularization or noise as causes when capacity is sufficient.

No measure of the share of polysemantic neurons in the diffusion model under different activation functions or architectures. Only SAE training losses are varied, and the SAEs are supervised on purpose.
No re-examination of canonical polysemantic neurons.
No comparison of activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

record.verdict_notes: The study mentions polysemanticity only as background. Its rows evaluate its own engineered SAE against a baseline SAE, so the reader's V5 link and labels are dropped. The paper explicitly uses 'neurons' and 'latents' interchangeably, which likely caused the mislink.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses diffusion-model cross-attention activations, not neurons in image classifiers such as InceptionV1.
No transformer language models or language-model neuron responses are measured.
The study does not test whether polysemanticity is caused by sparse-feature capacity pressure or superposition.
The study does not test initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of polysemanticity when capacity is sufficient.

It tests supervised versus unsupervised SAE training and some SAE loss variants in diffusion models, but not a broad sweep of activation functions or modern convolutional architectures, nor the share of polysemantic neurons in the original model.
It does not investigate whether canonical mixed-response neurons in the original sources have a shared feature, such as pose, or whether apparently unrelated inputs are related offshoots of one job.
It does not compare activation-range choices or explanation-scoring methods as alternate ways to classify a neuron as polysemantic.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: SAEmnesia feature-score and single-latent classification results; variants with reduced Cats-Dogs overlap
reader_labels.reason: The Flowers score has a dominant peak after supervised training, top-latent classification is described as nearly matching all features, and several SAE variants reduce measured overlap versus SAeUron (r02, r03, r08-r10, r12, r14, r16, r18).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Cats-Dogs overlap across SAE variants, especially fine-tuned variants
reader_labels.reason: Some variants show no overlap reduction, and one fine-tuned variant has more overlapping timesteps than the baseline; the paper also notes within-group interference (r11, r15, r17).
